01.event: A yavam and yevama who both admitted they had not consummated the levirate marriage came before Rava, who ordered halitza.
01.turn: Rav Sherevya objected that a baraita requires both a bill of divorce and halitza.
01.outcome: Rava conceded that if the baraita is taught, it stands, and retracted his ruling.
01.summary: A couple who both said their levirate marriage was never consummated came before Rava, and he told the court to arrange halitza and settle the case. Rav Sherevya objected that a baraita requires a bill of divorce as well as halitza. Rava answered that if that baraita is taught, then it stands, and he withdrew his ruling.

02.event: When his daughter's husband Abba (Gamliel's brother) died childless, Rabban Gamliel entered levirate marriage with her rival wife.
02.turn: The Gemara questions whether this proves anything, since Gamliel followed Beit Hillel, and then explains she was an aylonit.
02.outcome: No firm outcome; the incident is only used as a proof and then explained away.
02.summary: Rabban Gamliel's daughter was married to his brother Abba, who died childless, and Rabban Gamliel married her rival wife in levirate marriage. The Gemara first takes this as proof that rival wives of a daughter may do so, then notes Gamliel followed Beit Hillel and explains that the daughter was an aylonit, which changes the law.
02.missing: The incident is a one-line precedent cited for a legal argument and has no development beyond it.

03.missing: The passage cites a baraita about Michal and Jonah's wife only as a legal proof about time-bound mitzvot.

04.event: When Rav Naḥman came to Neharde'a he told the people to clear away the earth that had half-filled the entrances so the doors could be locked.
04.turn: The Gemara asks whether this shows he thinks doors must be locked.
04.outcome: It concludes he only required the doors to be fit for locking.
04.summary: The entrances of Neharde'a had been filled halfway with earth. When Rav Naḥman arrived he ordered the earth cleared away so the doors could be locked. The Gemara debates what this shows and concludes it only means the doors must be fit to be locked.
04.missing: The anecdote is a single instruction used as a legal proof, with no real action or resolution beyond the legal reading.

05.event: Captive women were lodged in his house with the ladder removed, and when one of them passed, he lifted a huge ladder alone and began climbing toward her.
05.turn: Halfway up he stopped himself, braced his legs and shouted that there was a fire in Amram's house.
05.outcome: The Sages came and he told them it is better to be shamed in this world; he made his evil inclination come out of him as a pillar of fire and told it he was still superior.
05.summary: Captive women redeemed in Neharde'a were lodged in Rav Amram's house with the ladder taken away. When one passed, her beauty lit up the opening, and Rav Amram lifted a ladder ten men could not move and began to climb. Halfway up he braced himself and shouted that there was a fire in his house, so the Sages came and saw him. He told them better to be shamed now than in the World-to-Come, and made his evil inclination leave him as a pillar of fire, telling it that he, though flesh, had prevailed over fire.

06.actor: The people of Neharde'a and Rav Naḥman
06.event: During a drought everyone in Neharde'a sold their mansions to buy wheat.
06.turn: Wheat arrived and the sales proved unnecessary.
06.outcome: Rav Naḥman ruled that the mansions be returned to their former owners.
06.summary: In a drought in Neharde'a, everyone sold his mansion to buy wheat. In the end wheat arrived, making the sales unnecessary, and Rav Naḥman ruled that the mansions go back to their original owners.

07.missing: The passage is a legal argument, with a short baraita quoted by Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok only as proof.

08.event: A man from Neharde'a insulted Rav Yehuda in a Pumbedita butcher shop, and Rav Yehuda excommunicated him and proclaimed him a slave.
08.turn: The man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Naḥman's court, where Rav Yehuda showed his superiority, and the man himself arrived and boasted of Hasmonean descent.
08.outcome: Rav Yehuda was vindicated by Rav Mattana's report of Shmuel; the man was publicized as a slave, marriage contracts were torn up, and Rav Yehuda escaped a stoning crowd by threatening to reveal their lineage.
08.summary: A man from Neharde'a insulted Rav Yehuda over the meat queue in Pumbedita, and Rav Yehuda excommunicated him and declared him a slave. The man summoned Rav Yehuda to Rav Naḥman's court. Rav Yehuda corrected Rav Naḥman's speech and refused his hospitality on technical grounds, then the sides questioned his rulings until the man arrived claiming royal Hasmonean descent. Rav Mattana confirmed Shmuel's ruling that anyone claiming this is a slave, and the man was publicly branded. Many marriages were annulled, and when a mob pursued Rav Yehuda to stone him, he threatened to reveal their own lineage and they dropped the stones.

09.actor: Rabba bar bar Ḥana and Rav
09.event: Rabba bar bar Ḥana gave Rav money to buy a plot of land for him, and Rav bought it for himself.
09.turn: A baraita calls such an agent's conduct deceitful, so the Gemara asks how Rav could do it.
09.outcome: The Gemara explains that the local violent landowners respected Rav but not Rabba, and that Rav feared someone else would buy the land if he took time to inform him.
09.summary: Rabba bar bar Ḥana gave Rav money to buy a plot of land for him, and Rav went and bought it for himself. The Gemara asks how he could, and answers that the sellers were violent men who honored Rav but not Rabba, and that Rav feared someone else would buy it while he went to inform Rabba.

10.missing: The passage describes a yard in Pum Nahara only as the setting for Abaye and Rava's legal proposals about side posts.

11.missing: The exchange is a halakhic argument between Rav Dimi and Abaye, with only a moment of silence and a compliment as incident.

12.event: A man helped Shmuel off a ferry and then said he had a case before him.
12.turn: The favor created a bond between them.
12.outcome: Shmuel disqualified himself from judging the man's case.
12.summary: Shmuel was crossing a river on a narrow ferry when a man gave him a hand to help him out. Shmuel asked what he was doing there, and the man said he had a case for him to judge. Shmuel said he was disqualified, because the man had done him a favor.

13.missing: The passage is a single piece of health advice from Elijah to Rabbi Natan, with no event.

14.event: Ulla, who often went up to Eretz Yisrael, died outside the Land.
14.turn: Rabbi Elazar mourned that he died in an unclean land, and when told his coffin was being brought to the Land, said it is not the same as being absorbed by its soil while alive.
14.outcome: Rabbi Elazar maintained that burial in the Land does not undo dying outside it.
14.summary: Ulla often ascended to Eretz Yisrael but died outside it. When Rabbi Elazar was told, he said the verse about dying in an unclean land was fulfilled through him. They told him Ulla's coffin was coming for burial in the Land, but he answered that being absorbed by its soil while alive is not the same as after death.

15.actor: Rabban Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva
15.event: Their boat set sail on Shabbat; Gamliel and Elazar ben Azarya walked its whole length while Yehoshua and Akiva stayed within four cubits.
15.turn: The Gemara asks what the sages' stringency implies about whether the boat was moving.
15.outcome: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak uses it to argue that they did not disagree about a moving boat.
15.summary: Several sages traveling from Pelandarsin found their boat out at sea on Shabbat. Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya walked around the whole boat, while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva would not move beyond four cubits, choosing to be stringent. The Gemara uses the incident only as evidence in a legal argument.
15.missing: The incident is quoted for its legal implication and has no ending beyond the sages' differing behavior.

16.missing: The passage is Rabbi Zeira's report of a ruling he heard from Rabbi Asi in Eretz Yisrael, a legal citation rather than an event.

17.event: Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passed Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi as they studied, and they stood for him.
17.turn: He told them they need not, since they were ordained and he was not, and since the Torah does not stand before its students.
17.outcome: He released them from the obligation to stand.
17.summary: Rabbi Elai and Rabbi Ya'akov bar Zavdi were studying Torah when Rabbi Shimon bar Abba passed, and they stood up. He told them they did not have to, because they were ordained scholars and he was not, and because someone engaged in Torah study need not stand.

18.event: After Rav Anan's act caused a miscarriage of justice, Elijah, who used to visit him to teach Seder deEliyahu, departed.
18.turn: Rav Anan fasted and prayed and Elijah returned, but now appeared in frightening forms.
18.outcome: Rav Anan made a box, sat in it before Elijah, and learned the whole Seder, which is why there are a Major and a Minor Seder.
18.summary: Elijah used to visit Rav Anan and teach him the Seder deEliyahu. After Rav Anan's action led to a miscarriage of justice, Elijah left, and Rav Anan fasted and prayed until he returned, but then Elijah frightened him in terrifying forms. Rav Anan made a box, sat inside it before Elijah, and learned the whole Seder, which explains the Major Order taught before the incident and the Minor Order after.

19.event: A brewer betrothed a woman with sediment from the date beer he was making for someone else, and the owner told him to give her sharper sediment of better quality.
19.turn: The brewer asked Rava whether the owner's remark meant he had relinquished his rights.
19.outcome: Rava told him the owner's words applied only to teruma, so the woman was not betrothed.
19.summary: A brewer making date beer for someone betrothed a woman with its sediment. The owner found him and told him to use a sharper, better sediment. The brewer asked Rava whether that meant the owner had given up his rights, and Rava said no: such a remark counts only for teruma, so the sediment was still the owner's.

20.event: A man deposited seven pearls in Rabbi Meyasha's house, and Rabbi Meyasha died without saying whose they were.
20.turn: His family and the depositor disputed ownership before Rabbi Ami.
20.outcome: Rabbi Ami awarded the pearls to the depositor, because Rabbi Meyasha was not wealthy enough to own them and the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.
20.summary: A man left seven pearls tied in a sheet at Rabbi Meyasha's house, and Rabbi Meyasha died without saying who owned them. His family and the depositor came before Rabbi Ami, who ruled for the depositor. He reasoned that Rabbi Meyasha was not rich enough to own such gems and that the claimant gave a distinguishing mark.
